title: 3.2 · What does the data say? (Claims, predictions, models)
name: What does the data say? (Claims, predictions, models)
summary: Students test a model's prediction against results and refine it. In Data Detective's Model Makers they set a ramp rule with a slider, run five trials, compare, and change the rule; case 5, Game Balance, tunes a runner's jump so about 80 percent of 20 test runs finish, a preview of playtesting their own game. One device per student.
iCan: test a model's prediction against results
change the model when the results disagree, and test it again
materials: Paper Predictions kit (a book ramp, a toy car and a ruler per group, and a ramp rule card, for the twin or the block day)
doNow: It rained the last 3 Mondays. Will it rain next Monday? How sure are you, and what rule are you using to predict?
plan: Explore: the ramp rule, five trials, refine

warmup.why: two retrieval items from 3.1, one vocabulary item, one preview of today, one more from 3.1

do: Open Data Detective at Model Makers on the projector (Open game at this chapter). Case 1 is the ramp: the rule says distance = 2 × height. Set a height, read the prediction out loud, then run 5 trials.
Compare the trials with the prediction. Let the class change the rule with the slider, run 5 trials again and watch the error get smaller.
say: A model is a rule that predicts what will happen. A simulation runs the rule so we can check it against results.
When the results disagree with the model, we do not ignore the results. We refine the model and test again.
ask: The rule predicted one distance and every trial landed farther. Is the rule wrong, or were the trials unlucky? How many trials before you trust it?
explore.afterAsk: Take three answers. Agree that one trial can be unlucky, but five trials that all land farther are a pattern. Move the slider one step and run the trials again.
explore.bigIdea: A model is only as good as its last test: predict, compare, refine.

play.stretch: the chapter, then 3 stars; case 5 is Game Balance
play.solo: one device per student; a neighbor may read the results out loud, never touch your screen
lookFors: changing the rule after one trial
changing two things at once and not knowing which change helped
in Game Balance, tuning until one run finishes instead of about 16 of 20
play.misconception: One good trial does not prove a model: you compare it with many results, and when they disagree you change the model, not the data.
earlyFinishers: help a neighbor without touching their screen

discuss: How many trials before you trusted your rule?
In Game Balance, why test 20 runs instead of one? What does that tell you about testing a game you make?
showMe: One student shows Game Balance on the projector: the first jump rule, the 20 runs, the change and the 20 runs again.

unpluggedTwin.title: Paper Predictions: the ramp
materials: a ramp made from a book and a board
a ruler or a tape measure
a ramp rule card: distance = 2 × height
steps: Groups measure the ramp height and use the rule card to predict how far the car rolls.
Run 5 trials, measure each and write them in the table. Work out the average.
Compare the average with the prediction. If they disagree, change the number in the rule.
Change the height, predict with the new rule and run 5 more trials. Did the error get smaller?
Share: which group's rule fits best? Write it on the board with its error.

subPlan: Do Now on paper, 3 minutes: it rained the last 3 Mondays; will it rain next Monday, how sure are you, and what rule are you using?
